clue.text: A senatorship has been arranged for a dramatist

indicators.note: the letters of the words before have been arranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A theatre writer is set up with a seat in the senate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has been arranged' rearranges the twelve letters of A SENATORSHIP into the name of the Athenian comic playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristophanes was the great comic playwright of ancient Athens, author of The Frogs and Lysistrata.

clue.text: Net saga about father's side descendants

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A family saga written for the internet concerns the paternal line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' tells you to shuffle NETSAGA into a seven-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: Agnates are relatives traced through male ancestors only, the paternal line of kinship.

clue.text: What E. F. Benson protagonist did (not of his own will)

definitions.text: What E. F. Benson protagonist did (not of his own will)

parts.words: What E. F. Benson protagonist did (not of his own will)
parts.note: something a hero came by through a dead person's testament rather than by choice; 'his own will' plays on a legal will versus wishing

explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like it says the hero acted unwillingly; really it says the property came through someone else's will, not his own.
explanation.definitionFit: To come into property under a will is to receive it as an heir, not by one's own choice.

clue.text: Reason why duration not endless, as Huxley suggested in 1944

definitions.text: Reason why duration not endless, as Huxley suggested in 1944

parts.words: Reason why duration not endless, as Huxley suggested in 1944
parts.note: Aldous Huxley's 1944 novel is titled Time Must Have a Stop, so a fixed cap on how long something lasts is what he implies

explanation.walkthrough: The 1944 book is Aldous Huxley's Time Must Have a Stop; a cap on duration is why time stops.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed cap on allowed duration is what keeps any period from going on for ever.

clue.text: Quick looks, say, at Whitbread winner

indicators.note: say signals that the words are to be heard spoken rather than read as spelt

parts.note: quick looks are peeps, brief glances

explanation.surface: Glances are cast at the winner of a literary prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Claire Tomalin's biography of the seventeenth-century diarist won the Whitbread Book of the Year in 2002, so the diarist is the 'winner'. The Whitbread was a major British book prize.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomalin's life of the London diarist Samuel took the Whitbread prize, so his name stands for the prize-winning book.

clue.text: One involved in Spanish building has a glazed look

definitions.text: One involved in Spanish building has a glazed look

parts.words: One involved in Spanish building has a glazed look
parts.note: a glazed ceramic wall tile is part of many Spanish and Portuguese buildings, and it literally looks glazed

explanation.walkthrough: 'has a glazed look' suggests a dazed person; really it is a shiny painted tile.
explanation.definitionFit: An azulejo is the painted, glazed ceramic tile used to decorate walls in Spain and Portugal.

clue.text: Métier I modified for those honourably discharged

indicators.note: modified means changed in form, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A soldier changes career after leaving the service with honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modified' rearranges METIERI (the accent is ignored) into the plural Latin word.
explanation.definitionFit: Emeriti are professors and others retired with honour, keeping their title after leaving office.

clue.text: Jerome recorded those of Henry, describing injured Serb amid outbreaks of applause

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: ovations are bursts of clapping

indicators.note: injured means damaged, so the letters of the word are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: A writer notes a wounded Serbian soldier being cheered.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerome K. Jerome wrote The Observations of Henry (1901), about a waiter. 'describing' is only a link word here; 'injured' is the anagram signal and 'amid' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome K. Jerome's 1901 book is titled after the remarks and comments of a waiter called Henry.

clue.text: English philosopher seems crooked, and a bad actor, too

parts.note: crooked means bent, not straight or dishonest
a ham is an actor who overacts badly

explanation.surface: A thinker is called both dishonest and a poor performer.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Bentham was the founder of utilitarianism; 'seems' and 'and ... too' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeremy Bentham was the London thinker who founded utilitarianism.

clue.text: No clue, badly formulated after a quiet start, could identify French composer …

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning quietly

indicators.note: badly formulated means put together wrongly, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A crossword-setter hints vaguely at a French musician's name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a quiet start' puts P first; 'badly formulated' turns NOCLUE into OULENC.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Poulenc was a twentieth-century French composer, one of the group known as Les Six.

clue.text: Man of letters is well-upholstered

explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of letters' looks like a writer in general but means the Earl famed for his Letters to His Son.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Chesterfield wrote famous letters to his son; a chesterfield is also a deeply padded leather sofa.

clue.text: … but even his thirteenth rallentando had charm

indicators.note: had here means contained, so the answer is held within the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, the composer's thirteenth slowing passage was delightful.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from the Poulenc clue. The run is inside thirteENTH RALlentando; a rallentando is a musical slowing down.
explanation.definitionFit: To charm someone is to captivate or delight them completely.

clue.text: Fruitless, like Hamlet's goodly frame

explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet II.ii the prince says 'this goodly frame, the earth, seems to me a sterile promontory'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruitless means barren; Hamlet calls the earth, that goodly frame, a barren 'promontory' in his speech to Rosencrantz.

clue.text: The call made by Ian Hamilton

explanation.walkthrough: Ian Hamilton here is the British poet and editor, whose debut book of poems was called The Visit.
explanation.definitionFit: A call is a short social stop at someone's home; The Visit was the poet Ian Hamilton's first collection (1970).

clue.text: Engraving showing singer in her true colours?

parts.note: a mezzo is a mezzo-soprano, a female singer
a tint is a shade of colour, here the hue that is truly hers

explanation.surface: A print reveals a vocalist's real personality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'true colours' suggests real character; here it is just a tint, a colouring.
explanation.definitionFit: A mezzotint is a print made by roughening a copper plate to give tonal shading.

clue.text: Baptist's father at a loss for words

definitions.text: Baptist's father at a loss for words

parts.words: Baptist's father at a loss for words
parts.note: in Luke's Gospel the father of John the Baptist was struck dumb for doubting the angel until the boy was named

explanation.walkthrough: 'at a loss for words' is literal: the priest was made mute until John's birth.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Gospel of Luke the priest who fathered John the Baptist is struck speechless by the angel Gabriel.

clue.text: "This is an important book, ——assumes, because it deals with war" (Virginia Woolf)

definitions.text: "This is an important book, ——assumes, because it deals with war" (Virginia Woolf)

parts.words: "This is an important book, ——assumes, because it deals with war" (Virginia Woolf)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Woolf's A Room of One's Own, where the gap is the reviewer who judges books

explanation.walkthrough: The gap is filled from Woolf's A Room of One's Own; the phrase is also the title of a Sheridan comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A reviewer who judges books is the person Woolf imagines making that assumption about war novels.

clue.text: "My duty then, shall pay me for my pains: / I will no more —— mine office on you" (All's Well That Ends Well)

definitions.text: "My duty then, shall pay me for my pains: / I will no more —— mine office on you" (All's Well That Ends Well)

parts.words: "My duty then, shall pay me for my pains: / I will no more —— mine office on you" (All's Well That Ends Well)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Helena's speech to the King, where the gap is a verb meaning to press or impose

explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is from Helena's speech to the King in All's Well That Ends Well, Act II scene i.
explanation.definitionFit: To press or impose a service upon someone is the sense Helena gives when she offers to stop urging her cure.

clue.text: Pianist better off keeping time

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: better off means richer, wealthier

explanation.surface: A keyboard player earns more by staying in tempo.
explanation.walkthrough: Sviatoslav Richter was a celebrated Soviet pianist.
explanation.definitionFit: Sviatoslav Richter was one of the great Soviet concert pianists of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Iachimo was, as it were, posthumously forgiven for winning one by deceit

definitions.text: Iachimo was, as it were, posthumously forgiven for winning one by deceit

parts.words: Iachimo was, as it were, posthumously forgiven for winning one by deceit
parts.note: in Cymbeline Iachimo wins a bet on Imogen's chastity by trickery and is pardoned at the end, after she was thought dead

explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Cymbeline, Iachimo bets Posthumus that Imogen can be seduced; 'posthumously' puns on Posthumus forgiving him.
explanation.definitionFit: A bet is what Iachimo makes with Posthumus over Imogen's fidelity, and he wins it by fraud.

clue.text: According to Shaw, he said that he was sorry for "the poor girl" (Saint Joan)

definitions.text: According to Shaw, he said that he was sorry for "the poor girl" (Saint Joan)

parts.words: According to Shaw, he said that he was sorry for "the poor girl" (Saint Joan)
parts.note: in Shaw's play Saint Joan it is the English earl who expresses sympathy for the poor girl Joan

explanation.walkthrough: In Shaw's Saint Joan the English nobleman Richard de Beauchamp, Earl of the title, speaks of 'the poor girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: The English earl in Shaw's Saint Joan is the character who voices pity for Joan at her trial.

clue.text: Laud, as might archbishop

explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Laud' hides the verb behind William Laud, Charles I's Archbishop of Canterbury.
explanation.definitionFit: To laud is to praise highly; an archbishop might extol God, and William Laud was Archbishop of Canterbury.

clue.text: He had a pressing duty in Restoration comedy

definitions.text: He had a pressing duty in Restoration comedy

parts.words: He had a pressing duty in Restoration comedy
parts.note: Farquhar's play The Recruiting ___ features a man who signs up soldiers, and pressing means press-ganging into service

explanation.walkthrough: 'pressing' means press-ganging men into the army, not urgent. The play is George Farquhar's The Recruiting Officer (1706).
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Plume in Farquhar's comedy is an army man enlisting soldiers, the title role of The Recruiting Officer.

clue.text: Radical stuff from Wesker

explanation.walkthrough: Arnold Wesker was a British playwright whose trilogy includes Roots (1959).
explanation.definitionFit: Radical relates to origins, the base of a plant or idea; Arnold Wesker wrote the 1959 play of that name.

clue.text: A poet I recognize from previous knowledge

parts.note: Matthew Prior was an English poet of the early eighteenth century

explanation.surface: A versifier says he can tell from what he already knows.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Matthew Prior (1664-1721); 'recognize' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin phrase for reasoning from known causes or principles before experience.

clue.text: Quick coda totters badly

indicators.note: badly means in a poor way, so the letters of the word are disordered

explanation.surface: The music's fast ending wobbles unsteadily.
explanation.walkthrough: A stretto is a closing passage played faster, or overlapping entries in a fugue.
explanation.definitionFit: In music a stretto is a final passage taken at a faster tempo, a speeded-up coda.

clue.text: First illuminated in early manuscripts

explanation.walkthrough: Medieval scribes decorated the big capital letter at the start of a text, the illuminated letter.
explanation.definitionFit: First means opening or earliest; a decorated opening capital letter was often painted in medieval books.

clue.text: Loud feature is the opener in Maclean work

parts.note: F is the musical abbreviation for forte, meaning loud
an ear is a facial feature
taken as written
a key opens a lock

explanation.surface: A noisy element is what unlocks a novelist's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Alistair MacLean's 1961 thriller is titled Fear is the Key.
explanation.definitionFit: Alistair MacLean, the Scottish thriller writer, published this novel in 1961.
